segments.narration: Twenty thousand tons of steel folded into the river. In August 1907, the majestic Quebec Bridge was supposed to shatter world records, not shatter into pieces.
Weeks before the disaster, riveters heard terrifying groans echo through the girders. Massive steel chords on the main anchor arm were visibly buckling, bending three inches out of straight.
Though warning signs mounted, communication breakdowns and delayed reactions meant the order to halt work arrived too late.
The math was fundamentally flawed from day one. Designers severely underestimated the massive dead weight of the cantilever structure, loading an unsupported frame far past its breaking point.
Eighty-six workers fell with the iron. That fatal miscalculation completely rewrote global engineering safety standards forever.

accuracy_flags.claim: Engineers ignored the warning signs and kept adding weight to the span.
accuracy_flags.note: While the consulting engineer Theodore Cooper initially brushed off the concerns as minor and delayed acting, the text notes he ultimately telegraphed to stop adding load once he met with McLure, though the message arrived too late. The script frames it as willful hubris by engineers actively keeping workers on the bridge, which oversimplifies the communication failure.

verdicts.claim: Twenty thousand tons of steel collapsed into the St. Lawrence River in 1907.
verdicts.note: The reference article mentions the collapse of the south arm and part of the central section into the St. Lawrence River in 1907, but it does not specify the exact tonnage of steel.

verdicts.claim: Construction workers had already noticed massive steel beams bending out of shape weeks prior.
verdicts.note: The reference states that the QBRC site engineering team began noticing increasing distortions of key structural members already in place in the summer of 1907, and McLure wrote repeatedly to Cooper as problems grew.

verdicts.claim: Engineers ignored the warning signs and kept adding weight to the span.
verdicts.note: While the consulting engineer Theodore Cooper initially brushed off the concerns as minor and delayed acting, the text notes he ultimately telegraphed to stop adding load once he met with McLure, though the message arrived too late. The script frames it as willful hubris by engineers actively keeping workers on the bridge, which oversimplifies the communication failure.
verdicts.correction: Though warning signs mounted, communication breakdowns and delayed reactions meant the order to halt work arrived too late.

verdicts.claim: A fatal calculation error regarding the dead weight of the cantilever design caused the collapse.
verdicts.note: The reference states the bridge's dead load proved too heavy, with its own weight exceeding carrying capacity, and the Royal Commission attributed failure to errors in judgment by designers P.L. Szlapka and Theodore Cooper.

verdicts.claim: The disaster resulted in standardizing modern structural engineering safety codes worldwide.
verdicts.note: The reference mentions the death toll (75 workers on the day of the 1907 collapse, out of 86 present) and the Royal Commission inquiry, but does not explicitly mention the creation of global engineering safety standards.
